name: Ben Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at a large mine, starting with a walk round the tyres before loading begins. I came into this job late and I'm still junior, so I check the route board twice and ask when a warning light puzzles me. I like the quiet focus of driving, and I use an AI search on my phone most days to find the right page of a manual, then check with the mechanic before touching anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the pit crew that a handy phone answer is no replacement for seeing a loose pin on a haul truck. AI can help me look up a fault code, but the mine still needs someone who will stop the machine and check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm pleased if the big claims fade, because I only joined this mine recently and I'm still slow at some checks. I have about four months of expenses saved, and my partner's wages help, but I don't want to call that a retirement fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my paid truck shifts and use the fault manual on my phone when I find a code I don't recognise. This winter I'll record the common faults in a notebook and ask our mechanic to correct my notes, so I get faster without guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel reasonably calm about the work itself. The pension question still sits in the background, but my partner and I can pay the regular bills right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made you start writing down faults?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the dashboard showed a code I'd seen once before, and I wasted ten minutes finding the right page. Our mechanic Sal showed me where to look, so the notebook is my way of remembering it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home if the picture stays quiet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Leena that I'll keep earning and we should talk through retirement numbers after the next bank statement. Our children are grown and supporting themselves; we don't need to make a grand family announcement.

say: I would say a **fault code** still needs a person to inspect the truck.
I would tell the crew that small **AI help** can speed up a manual search.
think: I am glad major change fades while I am still **learning checks**.
Our **four-month cushion** is useful but cannot stand in for retirement income.
do: Keep working **paid truck shifts** through the first year.
Use the **fault manual** and ask a mechanic to correct my notebook.
feel: Calm about current **work**, with retirement figures still unresolved.
S0.quote: AI can help me look up a fault code, but the mine still needs someone who will stop the machine and check it.
fieldNote: His ordinary use of **AI tools** already helps him find information, while he insists on checking the vehicle himself.
He feels secure in current **household bills**, but treats four months of savings as a limited retirement cushion.

steps.text: Keep taking paid haul-truck shifts through the first year
Use AI and the fault manual to identify unfamiliar truck codes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the dispatch office will change before the cabs do, and we should learn the new system instead of laughing at the office staff. The mine can gain from better routes, but a driver ought to be able to question a route that looks unsafe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the easier thinking work might let management cut the dispatcher who catches our mistakes. I'm junior and still learning, so a bad instruction on my screen could become my problem long before a robot touches the steering wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a trial of the new route screen with a supervisor beside me, and I'll practice flagging a blocked road. I'll carry on driving, and in the first year of the change I'll put aside one extra shift's pay when I can, since I don't know if new targets will trim hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel keen to try the route screen and worried about who is checking it. A tool that saves time can still leave the person in the cab with the blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an unsafe instruction look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After rain the north ramp can be slick, even when a map shows it as open. I'd want a clear button to tell dispatch about the ramp before another truck follows me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you speak to if the screen were wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First the shift supervisor, because a driver shouldn't improvise alone on a busy road. Then I'd sit with the dispatcher and show exactly where the route screen misled us.

say: I would say **dispatch** will change before driving does.
I would argue that drivers must be able to **challenge unsafe routes**.
think: I fear easier office work could remove a **dispatcher** who checks our mistakes.
As a **junior driver**, I could carry blame for a bad screen instruction.
do: Try the **route screen** beside a supervisor and practice flagging hazards.
Continue **truck shifts** while drivers remain needed.
Save an **extra shift’s pay** when available.
feel: Keen to experiment, but worried about **unchecked routes**.
S1.quote: A tool that saves time can still leave the person in the cab with the blame.
fieldNote: He welcomes the **route tool** while identifying a specific safety gap and a possible loss of dispatcher oversight.
His extra saving depends on **available shifts**; he expects possible targets to make hours less reliable.

steps.text: Practice flagging blocked mine roads on the route screen with a supervisor
Keep driving paid truck shifts while drivers are needed
Save one extra shift’s pay when shifts are available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office could be running on thinking AI by 2028, but our haul trucks would still need hands until about 2031. I'd ask for real dates from the company rather than a speech about innovation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60, when the thinking system arrives, I could still drive; at 63, if capable robots are ready, my junior place is exposed. I know how to use digital tools, but using a screen doesn't mean I know enough to repair an autonomous truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the maintenance lead about the electrical apprenticeship and the entry test; I'll apply if the mine pays the course fees and allows paid shifts. If AGI arrives in 2028, I'll keep driving during the three-year gap, save whatever overtime is actually offered, and apply to the regional bus depot if truck shifts start disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a jolt of fear and also an urge to get moving. Two years is tight for a man learning the job at 58, and I can't put our bills on my partner alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the bus depot take you without another licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know; I would ask them before filling out a form. A bus is different from a haul truck, and I'd rather hear the licence rule early than spend money blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the plan to your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Leena that I'll pursue the apprenticeship only if the wages and fees work. She earns, but her pay doesn't cover both of us, and I won't pretend a second career is free.

say: I would tell the crew that **2028** affects the office before robots reach the trucks.
I would ask the company for **real dates** for its robot plans.
think: I expect my **junior driving place** to be exposed around 2031.
Using a digital screen does not qualify me to **repair robots**.
do: Ask about the **electrical apprenticeship** and apply if fees and wages are covered.
Keep driving during the **three-year gap** after 2028.
Ask the **bus depot** about licences if truck shifts fall.
feel: Afraid of a **tight deadline**, but eager to act.
S2.quote: I know how to use digital tools, but using a screen doesn't mean I know enough to repair an autonomous truck.
fieldNote: He distinguishes his comfort with **digital tools** from the technical skill required to maintain autonomous vehicles.
His apprenticeship is **conditional** on paid shifts and covered fees; bus driving is a fallback if mine hours fall.

steps.text: Apply for the electrical apprenticeship if the mine covers fees and preserves paid shifts
Keep driving haul trucks during the gap after 2028
Apply to the regional bus depot if mine shifts fall and licence rules allow
Save offered overtime pay toward household expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to put an apprenticeship on the table while we still have people to teach it. Thinking AI may run the office in 2031, and robots may drive trucks around 2034; our crew should know which work stays paid in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 at the first date and 66 at the second. I can't count on retiring at 66, because my partner and I haven't checked what our income will be, and four months of savings won't bridge a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll book a meeting with the retirement adviser this year to get an estimate in writing. I'll request a place on the mine's electrical course if it is paid, continue driving while the trucks have operators, and in the first year after 2031 I'll compare posted maintenance and bus jobs before deciding which to apply for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels workable if I can keep wages coming in. I still feel uneasy about whether a short course leads to a real job, rather than just a certificate on the shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which course detail matters most to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to know who taught it and whether the mine has a maintenance vacancy at the end. I don't mind exams, but I won't give up paid hours for a paper nobody hiring asks for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you choose the bus depot instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine has no paid maintenance opening and the bus depot lists a job I can qualify for, I'd apply there. I would drive a bus rather than wait at home for a mine vacancy that doesn't exist.

say: I would say the mine has time for a **paid apprenticeship** before 2031.
I would ask which **truck work** stays paid until robots arrive around 2034.
think: I cannot assume **retirement at 66** without a written income estimate.
Our **four-month savings** would not cover a long employment gap.
do: Get a written **retirement estimate** this year.
Request a **paid electrical course** while driving shifts continue.
Compare actual **maintenance and bus vacancies** after 2031.
feel: Uneasy about whether training leads to **paid work**, despite more time.
S3.quote: I would drive a bus rather than wait at home for a mine vacancy that doesn't exist.
fieldNote: He uses the longer warning to seek **written numbers** and a course connected to an actual maintenance opening.
He makes bus work a **specific alternative** only if the mine lacks a paid role and the licence fits.

steps.text: Request the mine electrical course if fees and driving wages are covered
Continue paid haul-truck shifts while operators are needed
Apply for a suitable bus depot vacancy if mine maintenance work is unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger drivers to learn the equipment and keep their options open; 2036 for thinking AI and about 2039 for capable robots gives them time. I wouldn't tell them to wait for an employer to plan their whole working lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 68 when the office changes and 71 when a robot might drive my truck. I expect to reduce my own shifts before then if our retirement figures allow, but I'm not going to write 'retired' on the calendar without those figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working for now, ask for the written retirement estimate, and set a yearly date with my partner to review bills and savings. If we can cover the basics without my full wage, I'll move to fewer shifts before 2039; if we cannot, I'll keep applying for paid work I can still physically do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more settled with this version. The main worry is my health deciding the timetable before any machine does, so I need a plan that survives a bad knee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger driver at the mine gate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a younger driver to ask the mechanic how the truck works, not just which buttons to press. They have decades ahead; I have to be honest about my shorter runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the written estimate is lower than you hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would keep our older car and put off the long trip we have talked about. I'd also keep taking paid shifts while my knee permits, rather than leaning on our grown children.

say: I would urge younger drivers to **learn equipment** during the long warning.
I would say **2036 and 2039** give the crew different dates to prepare for.
think: I may reduce shifts before robots arrive at **71**, if income allows.
My **health** may limit driving before technology does.
do: Continue **paid truck work** while physically able.
Review **retirement figures** and household bills yearly with my partner.
Keep the **older car** and defer the trip if income is lower than expected.
feel: More settled, while alert to **knee trouble** and income uncertainty.
S4.quote: I'm not going to write 'retired' on the calendar without those figures.
fieldNote: He sees the long horizon as more relevant to **younger drivers**, while his own health and finances guide his exit.
He will reduce work only after a **written estimate** shows that the household can cover basic expenses.

steps.text: Continue paid haul-truck shifts while physically able
Keep the older car and defer the trip if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my driving may only have until around 2031 and I'm still learning this job. A paid electrical apprenticeship linked to a real maintenance vacancy would help, along with an honest company timetable and a written retirement estimate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether my partner wants the same plan. Leena is willing to talk numbers with me, but she also wants us to take that long trip while we can still enjoy it; work isn't our only clock.

headlineQuote: The main worry is my health deciding the timetable before any machine does, so I need a plan that survives a bad knee.
portrait: Ben is a **58-year-old junior** haul-truck driver who entered mining late and is still learning equipment checks.
He uses **AI search daily** for manuals, then checks uncertain answers with a mechanic.
His partner earns, but **four months** of saved expenses cannot fund a long job gap.
He seeks **paid technical training**, actual vacancies and written retirement figures before changing course.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only until around 2031 for him to replace possible driving income.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid electrical apprenticeship** tied to a real vacancy, clear dates and a written retirement estimate would help.
